clue.text: See 22
Hungry, so certain to eat 1 in 10 stew

indicators.note: to stew is to cook into a jumble, so the letters gathered here are mixed up

parts.note: certain means sure
1 is the Roman numeral I
10 is ten spelt out

explanation.surface: Someone so hungry they are bound to eat a tenth of the stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so' and 'to eat ... in' only dress the surface of a meal; the numbers are not quantities of stew but letters, the Roman one and ten written out.
explanation.definitionFit: Esurient is a literary word for greedy or famished, a straight synonym of hungry.

clue.text: See 20
See 10
Unseemly kid with light he's thrown

indicators.note: thrown suggests things scattered about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: read as he is: the word he, with is as a link

explanation.surface: A naughty youngster tossed about with a lamp by a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thrown' scrambles KID, LIGHT and HE; 'he's' is read as 'he is', so the 'is' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: High-kilted means with the skirt hitched up high, hence immodest or indecorous, which is unseemly.

clue.text: An attempt to hold up influenza by a Muslim prince

parts.note: An gives the letter A

indicators.note: to hold means to contain, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: an attempt or try is a bid

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom, i.e. backwards

parts.note: flu is short for influenza

explanation.surface: Trying to stop the spread of flu with the help of an Islamic ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns FLU into ULF, which BID holds: B-ULF-ID, framed by A and A. ABULFIDA (Abu al-Fida) was a 14th-century Kurdish prince of Hama and historian.
explanation.definitionFit: Abulfida was a medieval Ayyubid ruler of Hama, so a historical Islamic prince.

clue.text: An ex-colleague of mine and her anagrams

indicators.note: anagrams used as a verb: the words beside it are rearranged

explanation.surface: The setter recalls a former fellow compiler, and her word puzzles.
explanation.walkthrough: Hendra was a fellow Guardian setter of Enigmatist's; 'anagrams' is the verb that rearranges AND HER.
explanation.definitionFit: Hendra is the pseudonym of a crossword setter who once set alongside this puzzle's compiler.

clue.text: All right to uncork the wine?

indicators.note: uncorking takes the top off a bottle, so the first letter of the wine is removed

parts.note: Tokay is a sweet Hungarian wine

explanation.surface: Asking permission to open the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: TOKAY is a sweet Hungarian wine; uncorking it drops its top letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: Okay is the everyday word for acceptable or satisfactory, a synonym of all right.

clue.text: Haile Selassie was very distant: take wine round

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for recipe, Latin for take

indicators.note: round means one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: Asti is an Italian sparkling wine
afar means very far away

explanation.surface: An emperor was remote, so someone passes him a glass of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take' is the R of a prescription (Latin recipe), and the clue's order is shuffled: the take-piece leads, then the wine goes round the far-off piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Before his coronation the Ethiopian emperor bore the title and name Ras Tafari.

clue.text: 20 3's 12 quick-fit staff nearly botched has some padding

parts.note: 12 across is a holiday, which is a break

indicators.note: padding is stuffing put inside, so one piece goes into the other
botched means messed up, so these letters are rearranged
nearly means the word falls just short, losing its last letter

parts.note: some means any, as in have you any
quick means fast

explanation.surface: Somebody's novella and a rushed fitting by workers, with some stuffing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 3's is Truman Capote's. STAF (staff nearly) with FIT is jumbled by 'botched' to ATTIFFS, and ANY is padded into it.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1958 novella by the American writer is the work meant by the cross-reference.

clue.text: Jolly subject to examine outside state

indicators.note: outside means this word goes round the rest

parts.note: to vet is to examine
a jolly is slang for a Royal Marine, RM
subject to, as in on condition, means on

explanation.surface: A cheerful subject has to be checked from outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' is old naval slang for a Royal Marine (RM), not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Vermont is one of the fifty US states, so an example of a state.

clue.text: See 22 down
Standard team? No, superior!

definitions.meaning: Standard is the name of a Belgian football club, called after its home city
a feudal lord to whom service is owed

explanation.surface: Is that the standard team? No, a better one!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' is the name of the club Standard Liège, not 'normal'.
explanation.definitionFit: A liege lord is the superior to whom a vassal owes allegiance; Standard Liège is the football club.

clue.text: Buddhist canon shows what to do with light fantastic, less familiarly?

parts.words: what to do with light fantastic
parts.note: Milton's line trip it on the light fantastic toe, so you trip it
aka, also known as, introduces a name used less familiarly

explanation.surface: The scriptures say how to dance, put more formally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trip the light fantastic' means dance, from Milton's 'trip it ... on the light fantastic toe': TRIP IT, then AKA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tripitaka, or Pali Canon, is the three-basket collection of Buddhist scripture.

clue.text: Lords relieve themselves in fashion?

parts.note: read as a phrase saying the act of passing water is all the rage, while the lords are the nobility as a body

explanation.surface: Aristocrats all going to the loo at once because it is trendy.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as THE PEE RAGE: urinating is 'the rage', i.e. in fashion; the whole thing means the lords collectively.
explanation.definitionFit: The body of lords, dukes, earls and other nobles is collectively called this.

clue.text: See 10
Mensa member, perhaps, titillates Uncle Dicky

indicators.note: dicky is slang for weak or unsound, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: A clever club member excites a dodgy relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky', British slang for faulty, rearranges TITILLATES UNCLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone devoted to the intellect, such as a high-IQ society member, is an example.

clue.text: Blowing a fuse with SA in decline

parts.note: something in decline is losing ground
SA, sex appeal, is also called it

explanation.surface: An electrical fault in South Africa as its fortunes fall.
explanation.walkthrough: SA is sex appeal, known as IT (as in the 'It girl'), not South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are idioms for flying into a rage and losing self-control.

clue.text: Cross, having to carry dress that's wet

indicators.note: to carry means to hold within, so one word goes inside

parts.note: cross means angry, irate
rig means to dress or kit out

explanation.surface: An angry person having to lug soaked clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: IRATE carries RIG: IR-RIG-ATE; 'wet' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To irrigate is to water land, i.e. to wet it, used as a verb.

clue.text: Bill from "PC World" — source: northern town

parts.note: Bill Gates, the Microsoft founder from the PC world
the head of a river is its source

explanation.surface: A bill from a computer retailer arrives, from a northern place.
explanation.walkthrough: PC World is a UK computer shop, but here it points to Bill Gates of Microsoft.
explanation.definitionFit: Gateshead is a town in Tyne and Wear in north-east England.

clue.text: Genuine fellow with top books penned

definitions.text: Genuine fellow with top books penned

indicators.note: penned means enclosed, so the run sits inside the other word

parts.note: genuine means true
a fellow is a man
a cap is a top or lid
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A real man who has written leading books.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a description of the writer too: a genuine man, at the top of the bestsellers, whose books are 'penned' by him.
explanation.definitionFit: Truman Capote, the American author, wrote books, which is the clue's hidden picture.

clue.text: This type shoots back

indicators.note: back means read the word in reverse

parts.note: shoots means fires

explanation.surface: A gunman who returns fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'type' is printing type, not a kind of person.
explanation.definitionFit: A serif is the small stroke on letters of a typeface, so part of printing type.

clue.text: Mud-filled hollow in Berkshire

definitions.meaning: a bog or swampy hollow full of mud
a town in the English county of Berkshire, west of London

explanation.surface: A muddy dip in an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: A slough is a boggy hollow, and Slough is a large town in Berkshire west of London.

clue.text: One getting more distressed carrying appropriate receptacle?

definitions.text: One getting more distressed carrying appropriate receptacle?

indicators.note: distressed means upset, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: an urn holds ashes, fitting for a funeral

explanation.surface: A grieving person holding the urn at a funeral.
explanation.walkthrough: MORE jumbled to MOER by 'distressed' holds URN: MO-URN-ER; the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A person at a funeral, upset and holding the ashes, is one who grieves.

clue.text: 20 3's volatile good-time girl stylishly having all

indicators.note: volatile means unstable, so the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: Someone's flighty party girl, dressed stylishly, having it all.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 3's means Truman Capote's: his heroine's visiting card reads this. 'volatile' scrambles all thirty letters of GOOD-TIME GIRL STYLISHLY HAVING ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: The visiting card of the heroine of Capote's novella bears exactly this inscription.

clue.text: An essential for marriage, orgiasts state

indicators.note: essential for says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Something vital for weddings, the revellers declare.
explanation.definitionFit: Georgia is a US state, and also a country, so an example of a state.

clue.text: General IQ getting on for fifty, on target

parts.note: g is the psychologists' symbol for general intelligence
nearing fifty is getting on, i.e. old

explanation.surface: An army officer's intelligence fading towards middle age, though still accurate.
explanation.walkthrough: In archery the gold is the bull's-eye, so a hit on the gold is on target.
explanation.definitionFit: The innermost ring of an archery target is the gold, so hitting it is dead on target.

clue.text: Mystic in water went with current

parts.note: went through the water is swam
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A holy man went swimming with the tide.
explanation.walkthrough: I is the standard symbol for electric current.
explanation.definitionFit: A swami is a Hindu religious teacher, a mystic or holy man.

clue.text: See 22 down
